name: Video frame size
seoDesc: Video frame size: work out total file size from the vertical pixels and the video length. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary: Give the Video frame size calculator the vertical pixels, the video length, the color depth and the frame rate and it returns total file size. It is built for whatever you happen to be working on. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Video frame size calculator work?
sections.html:
The Video frame size calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total file size in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the vertical pixels, the video length, the color depth and the frame rate.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in px.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hours / minutes / seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in bits. The unit chip switches it to any of the 26 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in fps.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in megabytes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 26 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Video frame size calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total file size=frame rate × one frame size × video length
Horizontal pixels=one frame size ÷ (color depth × vertical pixels)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Horizontal pixels = 1920, Vertical pixels = 1080, Color depth = 3 bit and Frame rate = 24 — it reports One frame size = 6220800 MB.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: One frame size = 6220800 MB should be roughly the size you expected from Horizontal pixels = 1920 and Vertical pixels = 1080.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in gigabytes, and convertible to any of the 26 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds
  • Data sizes, opening in bits
  • Data sizes, opening in megabytes
  • Data sizes, opening in gigabytes

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Video frame size calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the vertical pixels, the video length and the color depth — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Video frame size calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total file size, derived from the vertical pixels, the video length and the color depth. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Video frame size calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the vertical pixels, the video length, the color depth and the frame rate, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter video length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Video length opens in hours / minutes / seconds and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports One frame size = 6220800 MB. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Video frame size calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
